title: Book 3 — Thalia, Chapter 409
paragraphs: I was witness, moreover, to a great marvel, which the local inhabitants pointed out to me. Of the bones scattered about of those who fell in this fight — each side lying separately, since the bones of the Persians were heaped on one side, where they had been laid apart at the start, and those of the Egyptians on the other — the skulls of the Persians are so weak that if you hit them with just a pebble you will make a hole in them, while those of the Egyptians are so exceedingly strong that you would hardly break them by striking them with a large stone. The cause of this, they said — and I for my part readily believe them — is that the Egyptians from early childhood shave their heads, and the bone is thickened by exposure to the sun. This is also the reason why they do not become bald: for among the Egyptians you see fewer bald-headed men than among any other race. This, then, is why they have strong skulls. The reason the Persians have weak ones is that from infancy they keep their heads delicately in the shade by wearing tiaras, that is, felt caps. So much for that. I saw a similar thing at Papremis in the case of those who were slain along with Achaimenes son of Dareios, by Inaros the Libyan.
